baaja_summary.text: S. 5653 changes federal permitting to speed up projects. It narrows environmental reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act, limits some Clean Water Act reviews and permit terms, and shortens some Endangered Species Act consultation timelines. On energy, it gives the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission more power to permit some interstate power lines, tells it to set protections for ratepayers from very large power users such as data centers, drops permit requirements for onshore oil and gas drilling on nonfederal land, and speeds up renewable, geothermal, hydropower and offshore projects. It also limits the scope of National Historic Preservation Act reviews.

events.title: Government funding runs out, December 11
events.date_label: Friday, December 11, 2026 (funding ends at the end of the day)
what: The law that funds the federal government right now is a stopgap, Public Law 119-103, the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500), signed September 2, 2026. Section 106(3) says the money lasts through December 11, 2026.

Unless Congress passes new funding by then, parts of the government shut down. The same law also extends the National Flood Insurance Program and surface transportation (highway) programs to December 11, so those end too unless they are extended again.
Congress can pass another stopgap, a full-year bill, or let funding lapse. Funding bills start in the Appropriations Committees of the House and Senate.

events.title: Free federal court records: the Open Courts Act
events.date_label: Friday, January 1, 2027: the PACER fee rises from 10 to 12 cents a page
what: Federal court records are public, but most are not free. To read them online you use PACER, the federal courts' own system. It charges 10 cents a page, up to $3 for most documents. Anyone who runs up $30 or less in a quarter pays nothing.

On June 26, 2026 the Judicial Conference, which sets policy for the federal courts, approved a rise to 12 cents a page starting January 1, 2027. It lasts five years. The free amount goes up to $40 a quarter. The courts say the money pays for a new, more secure case system that will cost $700 million to $800 million over six years.

The Open Courts Act of 2026 (S. 4667) would replace PACER and the courts' filing system with one new system and make public court records free to read. Senator John Kennedy (R-La.) introduced it on June 2, 2026, with Senator Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) as cosponsor. It went to the Senate Judiciary Committee that day. The official record shows no action since.
Under the bill, users who spend more than $25,000 a quarter and federal agencies would still pay, according to Fix the Court, a group that supports it.

This is not new. The House passed the Open Courts Act of 2020 (H.R. 8235, from Representatives Hank Johnson, D-Ga., and Doug Collins, R-Ga.) on December 8, 2020, but the Senate never voted on it. A 2021 version did not pass either.
Any bill that has not passed both the House and the Senate when the new Congress begins on January 3, 2027 dies. S. 4667 would then have to be introduced again.

view.h: If you think court records should be free
p: You can ask your senators to support the Open Courts Act (S. 4667), and to bring it back in 2027 if it runs out of time. The "Write to your senators about this" link near the bottom of this page builds a letter with sourced facts.
You can read many records free today, and share the ones you buy so others can read them free too. See the free tools below.
If you think the courts need the fees to pay for a secure system, the same letter tool has the facts for that side too. The points on both sides are listed below the same way.

sides.h: What supporters of free records say
items: Sponsors come from both parties: Kennedy (R) and Wyden (D) in 2026, Johnson (D) and Collins (R) in 2020.
Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, December 11, 2020
Senator Wyden said the bill would save "more than $60 million" a year in operating costs.
Fix the Court cites IT experts who put a new free system at $10 million to $20 million to build and $3 million to $5 million a year to run.

Free Law Project says PACER took in $154.1 million in fees in 2025, and that the Congressional Budget Office estimated an earlier version would cut yearly operating costs from $64 million to $15 million.
In a lawsuit over PACER fees, a judge found the courts collected more than $920 million from 2010 to 2016. A $125 million settlement was approved in 2024 and upheld on appeal in March 2026.
Supporters say paying per page makes it harder for the public, reporters and researchers to check what courts do.
The courts say they share the goal: "We also share the goal that PACER be provided without charge to most ordinary users, which is already the case."
Judiciary analysis of the Open Courts Act of 2021 (H.R. 5844, S. 2614)
The Judicial Conference opposes paying for free PACER by raising filing fees. In 2020 it estimated filing fees would have to rise about $750 per case, taking the $350 civil filing fee to $1,100.
Judicial Conference letter to the House Judiciary Committee, September 23, 2020
It said 87 percent of PACER money comes from less than 3 percent of accounts.
Judicial Conference letter to the House Judiciary Committee, September 23, 2020
It says money from Congress is "neither stable nor predictable" and wants a reliable source in place before fees end.
Judiciary analysis of the Open Courts Act of 2021 (H.R. 5844, S. 2614)
Administrative Office letters to Rep. Hank Johnson, April 26 and September 27, 2021

In 2021 the head of the courts' administrative office wrote: "If PACER fees are eliminated without a sufficient replacement, we will be unable to successfully pursue this project," and said the bill could set a timeline "that is likely not feasible."
Administrative Office letters to Rep. Hank Johnson, April 26 and September 27, 2021

In June 2026 Judge Robert Conrad, who heads that office now, said: "without a modest increase in fees, we will not be able to collect enough money to cover the costs of delivering the case management system."
U.S. Courts, June 26, 2026: Judiciary approves funding for case management and public access modernization
We found no published judiciary position on the 2026 bill yet. The points above are about the 2020 and 2021 versions and the 2026 fee decision.

events.title: The new Congress begins, January 3, 2027
what: The 20th Amendment says the terms of senators and representatives end at noon on January 3 and the terms of their successors begin then.
Every House seat was on the ballot on November 3, 2026, so all 435 House terms end, and the winners take office. One third of the Senate was also up; the senators whose terms end are listed below.
Any bill that has not passed both the House and the Senate by then dies and must be introduced again in the new Congress.
